g.text: System design — a purchase summer, fully specified
one window, 6 firings: 8 → 15 → 15 → 15 → 15 → 19 · 11 values published under retraction
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · window [12:00, 12:02) = 19
PURCHASE SUMMING — FOUR STAGES AND FOUR ANSWERS
the four questions are answered across the last two stages
writer (event source)
emits a purchase stamped with its event time
transport (stream)
delays and reorders; also computes the watermark (max seen − 60s)
collector (window assigner)
assigns by event time to fixed 120s windows — WHERE
aggregator/store (per-window state)
running sum per window, held for allowed lateness — WHAT + WHEN + HOW
Window [12:00, 12:02) is the one this design is specified for: ids 0, 1, 2, 7, true sum 19.
One of those, id 7, arrives at 12:04:40 — 230s after it happened and after the window has already been published.
Step 1/4 — the pipeline, and the one window it is specified for
A deliberately small design, so every number is checkable. The four questions are not spread across the pipeline evenly: WHERE is the collector's
single rule, and WHAT, WHEN and HOW all live in the aggregator's state. That is also where every difficulty in this design is, which is why "where
is the state?" is the useful first question about any streaming system.
System design — a purchase summer, fully specified
one window, 6 firings: 8 → 15 → 15 → 15 → 15 → 19 · 11 values published under retraction
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · window [12:00, 12:02) = 19
WHAT A CONSUMER ACTUALLY RECEIVES, IN ORDER
one window, 6 firings, 11 published values
12:01:00 — EARLY pane 8
publishes 8 (nothing to undo yet)
12:02:00 — EARLY pane 15
publishes -8, then 15 (undo, then the new total)
12:03:00 — EARLY pane 15
publishes -15, then 15 (undo, then the new total)
12:04:00 — EARLY pane 15
publishes -15, then 15 (undo, then the new total)
12:04:06 — ON-TIME pane 15
publishes -15, then 15 (undo, then the new total)
12:04:40 — LATE pane 19
publishes -15, then 19 (undo, then the new total)
A sink that only adds ends at 19 — correct — because every refinement carries its own undo.
The "answer" to this query was published 6 times over 220s. That is not a malfunction; it is what answering a question about an unbounded stream
looks like.
Step 2/4 — the publish sequence, with real times
Read the column: 8, -8, 15, -15, 15, -15, 15, -15, 15, -15, 19. One query, one window, 11 published values across 220s, summing to 19 — and every
firing was the right answer to "what do you know now?". A consumer that treats the first as final is the bug, not the pipeline.
System design — a purchase summer, fully specified
one window, 6 firings: 8 → 15 → 15 → 15 → 15 → 19 · 11 values published under retraction
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · window [12:00, 12:02) = 19
THE TWO KNOBS, AND THEIR EXACT THRESHOLDS
two independent settings; one wrong value in either is enough
allowed lateness < 81s
id 7 discarded · final answer 15 · 21% low, permanently
allowed lateness >= 81s
id 7 accepted · final answer 19 · state held longer
accumulation = discarding, summing sink
19 — correct, and the cheapest to transmit
accumulation = accumulating, summing sink
87 — over-counted by 68
Neither knob is about performance. Allowed lateness decides whether 19 is reachable at all; accumulation decides whether the sink lands on 19 or
And they are independent: correct lateness with a mismatched sink still gives 87.
Step 3/4 — the two settings that decide whether it is ever right
Two settings, and each has a threshold that is a number rather than a judgement. Allowed lateness must be at least 81s — set by the watermark's
jump, not by id 7's 230s of skew. And the accumulation mode must match what the sink does with a pane. Get either wrong and the pipeline is still
"working".
System design — a purchase summer, fully specified
one window, 6 firings: 8 → 15 → 15 → 15 → 15 → 19 · 11 values published under retraction
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · window [12:00, 12:02) = 19
SCOPE
Allowed lateness >= 81s keeps window state alive longer. With 4 windows that is cheap; with a million open windows it is the memory bill.
Retractions require the sink to accept a negative. A counter in a key-value store usually can; an append-only billing ledger usually cannot.
The 81s threshold was computed from watermarks we can see in full. A live pipeline sets that number before observing them.
One window was specified. The window starting 12:08 never closes in this dataset: the on-time and late triggers never publish it.
Only the early trigger does — 8 at 12:10:00, then 8 again every 60s, since no on-time pane ever stops it.
Step 4/4 — and what this design does NOT settle
The sharpest gap: the final window is never published by the on-time or late trigger, because the watermark never passes its end. Only the early
trigger reports it — 8 at 12:10:00, then again every 60s, since no on-time pane ever stops it — and every value is speculative. Four answered
questions still say nothing about a window whose "when" never arrives.
